parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

**Heartfelt Greetings Ltd (HGL)**

Heartfelt Greetings Ltd (HGL) is a private limited company that designs and manufactures greetings cards in Country Y. Established 15 years ago, HGL has become known for its high-quality, hand-finished cards. The company employs 50 people and had sales revenue of \$5 million last year, with a profit of \$750,000.

HGL's cards are sold through independent gift shops and some national retail chains in Country Y. The company is considering expanding its operations to sell cards in neighbouring countries. To do this, HGL would need to increase its production capacity and invest in new printing technology.

The greetings card market in Country Y is becoming increasingly competitive. Many customers are switching to digital cards or using social media to send greetings, which has led to a 10% decline in physical card sales over the past two years. Additionally, the cost of raw materials, particularly high-quality paper, has increased by 15% in the last year due to supply chain disruptions.

HGL's Finance Director has prepared a cash flow forecast for the next six months (see Appendix 1). The forecast shows that while the business currently has a positive cash balance, it may face cash flow problems if it proceeds with its expansion plans without careful financial management.

The Managing Director is considering two options to finance the expansion:

1. Take out a long-term bank loan of \$2 million
2. Sell 25% of the company's shares to a venture capital firm

**Appendix 1: Six-month cash flow forecast for HGL (in \$000s)**

|   | **May** | **June** | **July** | **August** | **September** | **October** |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Opening balance** | 200 | 150 | 50 | (50) | (100) | 0 |
| **Cash inflows** | 400 | 350 | 300 | 400 | 500 | 600 |
| **Cash outflows** | 450 | 450 | 400 | 450 | 400 | 500 |
| **Net cash flow** | (50) | (100) | (100) | (50) | 100 | 100 |
| **Closing balance** | 150 | 50 | (50) | (100) | 0 | 100 |

Consider how the following three changes in HGL's cash flow forecast could affect the business.

- Increase cash inflows by \$100,000 per month
- Reduce cash outflows by \$75,000 per month
- Arrange an overdraft facility of \$200,000

Which change would have the greatest impact on HGL's working capital? Justify your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/heartfelt-greetings-ltd-case-study.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
Increasing cash inflows by \$100,000 each month could improve HGL's working capital position. They could purchase new machines to make new types of cards **[Ap]** or use it to fund advertising to tell more people about their cards. This could help them sell more, as they're currently selling 10% fewer cards **[Ap]** than before **[An]**

HGL could try to spend \$75,000 less each month. They might pay less for supplies or find cheaper ways to make cards, though if they cut too much, their cards might not be as attractive **[An]**. Customers like HGL's cards quality, finished-by-hand cards **[Ap]** and this option risks losing an important USP that attracts customers to HGL rather than rivals **[An]**

Another option is to get a \$200,000 overdraft, which could help in July and August when they expect to be low on cash** [Ap]**. However, borrowing money doesn't fix the problem of not having enough cash coming in, and overdrafts need to be paid back with interest, increasing costs **[An]**

Adding \$100,000 more cash each month would help HGL the most** [E]**. It gives them the most extra money to use and helps them make more money, not just spend less or borrow** [E]**. Spending less money might make their hand-made cards **[Ap]** less desirable, so people might stop buying them, hurting HGL's working capital position even more **[E]**. Similarly, borrowing money with an overdraft means HGL would have to pay it back later, making their money problems worse in the future **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Bank loan of \$2 million**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Maintains full ownership and control for existing shareholders
>     - Provides an immediate lump sum to finance capacity expansion and new printing technology
>     - Interest payments are tax deductible → reduces net borrowing cost
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Increases long-term debt obligations and fixed finance costs
>     - Adds monthly repayments that may worsen negative cash balances in July and August
>     - Requires collateral or personal guarantees → raises financial risk
>     - Limits future borrowing capacity for working capital
> - **Sell 25 % of shares to a venture capital firm**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Equity funding does not require repayment → avoids adding debt-service pressure in cash-poor months
>     - VC brings strategic expertise, networks and industry connections
>     - Strengthens the equity base → improves overall financial flexibility
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Dilutes existing ownership by 25 % → reduces control for current shareholders
>     - VC investors expect high returns and may push for aggressive growth targets
>     - Future dividends must be shared with new investors
> - **Recommendation**
> 
>   - Option 2 (venture capital investment) is most appropriate given the forecast cash-flow shortfalls in July–August
>   - Equity funding avoids extra debt repayments that the cash forecast shows the business cannot comfortably meet
>   - The VC’s expertise and network will support a successful expansion and offset the cost of dilution

**Extract:**

**HomeHardware Plus (HHP)**

HomeHardware Plus (HHP) is a chain of 50 hardware stores in Country X. It is a private limited company that has been operating for 25 years. HHP sells a wide range of DIY products, tools, and building materials to both individual customers and small construction businesses. The company has a centralized warehouse that supplies all its stores.

HHP has been facing increasing competition from online retailers. Its sales have declined by 10% over the past two years, and profits have fallen from \$5 million to \$3 million. The Finance Director has prepared a cash flow forecast for the next six months, which shows that HHP may face liquidity problems in the near future (see Appendix 1).

To address these challenges, HHP is considering launching its own e-commerce website. This would require an initial investment of \$2 million for website development, additional inventory, and staff training. The Marketing Director estimates that online sales could reach \$500,000 per month within the first year.

HHP's Human Resources Director believes that the company's 500 employees need to improve their customer service skills to compete effectively with online retailers. She has proposed a comprehensive training program that would cost \$200,000.

The company is also exploring the possibility of expanding into neighbouring Country Y, where the construction industry is booming. However, Country Y has recently introduced import quotas on building materials, which could affect HHP's supply chain.

**Appendix 1: Extract from HHP's projected monthly cash flow forecast (in \$000s)**

|   | **July** | **August** | **September** | **October** | **November** | **December** |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Cash inflows** | 2000 | 1800 | 1700 | 1600 | 1500 | 1400 |
| **Cash outflows** | 1900 | 1850 | 1900 | 1950 | 2000 | 2050 |
| **Net cash flow** | 100 | (50) | (200) | (350) | (500) | (650) |
| **Opening balance** | 500 | 600 | 550 | 350 | 0 | (500) |
| **Closing balance** | 600 | 550 | 350 | 0 | (500) | (1150) |

Consider how the following three changes in HHP's cash flow forecast might affect the business.

- A 20% increase in monthly cash inflows
- A 15% decrease in monthly cash outflows
- A \$1 million injection of capital in July

Which change would have the greatest impact on HHP's working capital? Justify your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/homehardware-plus-case-study.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
A 20% increase in monthly cash inflows would significantly improve HHP's working capital. Given current inflows of around \$1.5-2 million per month, this could provide an extra \$300,000-\$400,000 monthly **[Ap]**. This additional cash would help cover short-term debts and potentially eliminate the projected negative balances in November and December **[An]. **However, such an increase in sales** **may be unrealistic given HHP's recent 10% sales decline **[Ap]**

A 15% decrease in monthly cash outflows, currently around \$2 million, could save HHP approximately \$300,000 per month **[Ap]**. This would positively impact working capital by reducing cash leaving the business, helping maintain a positive balance and help HHP avoid liquidity issues **[An]**. However, it might involve job cuts, hurting employee morale and productivity

A \$1 million capital injection in July would immediately boost HHP's cash position and working capital. This large one-time inflow would provide a buffer against projected negative balances and support investments **[An]** in growth initiatives like the proposed \$2 million e-commerce website **[Ap]**

The \$1 million capital injection would likely have the greatest impact on HHP's working capital. While the other changes would improve cash flow incrementally, the large upfront boost would immediately improve HHP's liquidity **[E]**. Increasing monthly cash flows would be more gradual, so wouldn't solve HHP's immediate cash flow problems, and reducing cash outflows could negatively impact operations, potentially affect customer service **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **20% increase in monthly cash inflows**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - 20 % rise in inflows → each month’s net cash flow improves → boosts working capital buffer
>     - July inflows jump from \$2 000 k to \$2 400 k → July net cash moves from \$100 k to \$500 k → avoids early liquidity strain
>     - Higher inflows reduce risk of consecutive negative closing balances in Sept–Dec
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Sales growth needed to sustain 20 % increase may not materialise
>     - If outflows remain high, stronger inflows alone might not prevent liquidity shortages
> - **15% decrease in monthly cash outflows**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Cutting outflows by 15 % lowers monthly cash drain → net cash improves across all months
>     - October–December outflows of \$1 950–2 050 k fall by about \$292–308 k → negative months turn closer to break-even or positive
>     - Reduces need for external finance and interest costs
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - May require cuts to essential spending (staff, inventory) → risks harming operations
>     - Some costs (rent, utilities) are fixed and cannot be fully reduced
> - **\$1 million injection of capital in July**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - One-off \$1 000 k boost → July closing balance rises to \$1 600 k → strong cushion before downturn
>     - Covers shortfalls in Aug–Dec without changing day-to-day operations
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Does not address underlying cash flow issues → future months still run negative if operations unchanged
>     - Injection may come as debt or equity dilution → long-term financial cost
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - 15% reduction in outflows has the greatest impact on working capital by sustainably improving monthly net cash and reducing recurring cash deficits
>   - 20% inflow increase also helps but relies on uncertain revenue growth and may lag in effect
>   - \$1 million capital injection solves short-term gaps but fails to improve ongoing cash generation and leaves future deficits untouched

Zane and Zaara are both actors. They plan to start up a theatre in a low-income area of Main City. Zane and Zaara believe that helping the community is as important as being successful entrepreneurs.

In the daytime the theatre building will be used by Daycare, a local social enterprise. Daycare takes care of young children up to the age of 5 so that low-income family members can go out to work. **Soapy Sudds Manufacturer (SSM)**

SSM is a public limited company that was set up 25 years ago. SSM manufacture soap powder in country Y. The soap powder is used for washing clothes. SSM sells all its soap powder to large retailers in country Y. SSM’s sales have been increasing for many years in country Y but sales in the last year have remained the same. The directors of SSM are considering ways to increase sales.

SSM has a total of 100 employees with 60 in the Operations Department. It uses flow production in the factory and has 10 production lines with 5 workers and 1 supervisor for each line. The Operations Manager is aware that production workers are unhappy and often complain about their jobs being boring. These workers have always been paid by an hourly rate. The Human Resources Manager has recommended changes to ensure fewer workers leave each year to work for other businesses.

The directors of SSM have decided to expand the factory. They will need \$15m to do this. The directors have also considered taking over a competitor. SSM is likely to benefit from economies of scale as it grows.

The Marketing Director thinks SSM should start selling soap powder in markets in other countries. SSM will need to carry out either primary market research or secondary market research to forecast the potential total sales in these new markets. There are many existing manufacturers in these countries. SSM need to consider the problems when entering new markets in other countries such as tariffs or quotas.

{align=center} **Appendix 1**

{align=center} **Manufacturing process to make soap powder**

All the different types of soap powder are manufactured on production lines using flow production. SSM makes use of specialisation.

Each production line has the following stages:

![Flowchart of soap powder production: Stage 1 - raw materials mixed; Stage 2 - released onto conveyor belt; Stage 3 - packaged; Stage 4 - quality checks; Stage 5 - stored.](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/45154_nov-2021-paper-2-case-study.png)

Each of these stages uses machinery controlled by a production worker

{align=center} Appendix 2

{align=center} Email from the SSM Finance Director to the Managing Director

SSM has a cash-flow problem which may get worse. Please see charts below

![Two bar graphs comparing days taken to pay SSM (left) and SSM paying suppliers (right) from 2019 to 2021. Both graphs show increasing trends.](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/27918_nov-2021-paper-2-case-study-2.png)

{align=center} **Appendix 3**

{align=center} **Newspaper article from Main News 1 October 2021**

Retailers have reported increased sales for most types of products such as sales of washing machines which have increased by 15%. Economic growth in country Y is predicted to increase.

Many businesses have been recruiting additional employees and there are now shortages of some skilled workers. The government in country Y has recorded an increase in inflation to 8% so far this year, which is a worry.

Explain two ways SSM’s cash-flow problems could be overcome.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/nov-2021-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Firstly, SSM could ask customers to pay more quickly **[K]**. Debtors in 2021 take 60 days to pay SSM, up from 20 days in 2019 **[Ap]**. By reducing this back to 20 days, SSM would receive cash inflows much faster **[An]**. This would increase the amount of cash available to SSM to pay its own bills and suppliers **[An]**

Secondly, SSM could delay payments to its suppliers **[K]**. SSM currently pays suppliers in 20 days, down from 40 days in 2019. By extending this back to 40 days **[Ap]**, SSM would reduce its cash outflows in the short-term. This would allow SSM to hold onto cash for longer before having to pay suppliers **[An]**, easing pressure on its working capital and improving its liquidity position **[An]**

>   - Delay payment to suppliers – as it used to be 40 days and is now 20 days–cash outflow decreases – less working capital required so eases cash flow problem
>   - To ask customers to pay promptly – instead of waiting 60 days – cash flows into the business more quickly – may have time to receive revenue from sales before payment for raw materials is necessary
>   - Delay or cancel purchases of capital equipment – delay paying out the\$15 million for expansion – reduces cash outflow in the short-term
